reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AABB Technical Manual
clinicalPearls: Presents as acute hypoxaemia and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema developing during or within about six hours of transfusion
Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates appear on chest imaging without evidence of left atrial hypertension or fluid overload
A key distinction from TACO is the absence of features of circulatory overload; jugular venous pressure and natriuretic peptides are typically not elevated
Often mediated by donor anti-leukocyte (anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil) antibodies, so plasma-rich components from multiparous or previously transfused donors carry higher risk
Historically a leading cause of transfusion-related mortality, which fell substantially after mitigation strategies such as using predominantly male-donor plasma
Management is supportive with oxygen and lung-protective ventilation as needed; diuretics are unhelpful and the picture is one of capillary leak rather than volume excess
Most patients improve within one to three days, distinguishing it from other causes of ARDS
reference.pathophysiology: TRALI reflects acute injury to the pulmonary capillary endothelium leading to increased permeability and protein-rich alveolar oedema. A widely used two-hit model proposes that a predisposing condition (such as sepsis, surgery, or inflammation) primes and sequesters neutrophils in the lung; a second hit from transfused antibodies against recipient leukocyte antigens, or from biologically active lipids and cytokines accumulated in stored components, then activates these neutrophils. The resulting release of reactive oxygen species and proteases damages the endothelium and produces non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes
Bacterial contamination of a component with sepsis
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph or CT showing bilateral infiltrates
Arterial blood gas or pulse oximetry to quantify hypoxaemia
Natriuretic peptide levels and echocardiography to help exclude circulatory overload
Investigation of implicated donors for anti-HLA and anti-neutrophil antibodies via the transfusion service
Exclusion of infective and cardiac causes
redFlags: Acute severe hypoxaemia and respiratory distress during or shortly after transfusion requiring urgent oxygen and possible ventilatory support
Rapid clinical deterioration necessitating critical care
Diagnostic uncertainty with concurrent features of overload or sepsis
Recurrence on re-exposure to a component from an implicated donor
reference.prognosis: Most cases resolve within one to three days with supportive care and hypoxaemia improves, but severe episodes can be fatal; identification and deferral of implicated donors prevents further cases.
pitfalls: Misattributing the picture to fluid overload and giving diuretics, delaying appropriate supportive care
Failing to stop the transfusion and report the reaction to the transfusion service
Not investigating and deferring implicated donors, risking further cases
Overlooking TRALI in ventilated critically ill patients where hypoxaemia is attributed solely to underlying illness
management: Stop the transfusion immediately and notify the transfusion service when acute hypoxaemia develops within hours of a component
Supportive respiratory care with supplemental oxygen, escalating to non-invasive or lung-protective invasive ventilation for the non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Support the circulation with fluids and vasopressors for hypotension, recognising this is capillary leak rather than volume overload
Avoid diuretics, which are unhelpful because the oedema is inflammatory and permeability-driven rather than hydrostatic
Report the reaction and investigate implicated donors for anti-HLA and anti-neutrophil antibodies, deferring them to prevent further cases
Preventive transfusion practice using predominantly male-donor plasma and restrictive component use to lower risk
